cards.value_why: India has influencer-specific disclosure rules (ASCI, the Consumer Affairs Endorsement Know-hows), which shows the volume of this work; no single marketplace category isolates it (harvest). Brands now convert creator posts into paid partnership ads (Meta, 2026), raising the stakes on the copy.
cards.goal: Followers engage with the post as the creator's content (save, click the link, use the code) and know it is a paid partnership.

structure.does: A permitted label in the first line, above the 'more' cut ('Ad | Paid partnership with @brand'), plus the platform's paid-partnership tag.
Opens the way this creator always opens: a moment, a confession, a question from their audience.
How the creator actually used the product, with one detail only a real user would know (time of day, the routine it replaced).
What worked, in the creator's words, using only claims the brand has substantiated; one honest limit or 'who it's not for' if the creator would say it.
Code or link, what it gives, deadline.
Brand handle, up to 5 hashtags; for video, 3-6 bullet talking points with must-say claims and don'ts, not a word-for-word script.

length.note: Caption length follows the creator's usual style; a creator who writes two lines should not suddenly post 250 words for a brand. Talking points are separate from the caption.

checklist: Is a permitted disclosure label in the first line, visible without tapping 'more'?
Is the platform's paid-partnership tag noted in addition to the written label?
Does it sound like this creator (their openings, slang, sentence length), not the brand's website?
Is there one specific detail of real use?
Are all product claims from the brand's approved, substantiated list?
For health, nutrition or finance topics, is the creator's relevant qualification stated upfront, or the claim removed?
Is there one CTA with the code or link and what it gives?
Are there 5 or fewer hashtags?
Does it avoid disparaging competitors by name?
If any visual or voice is AI-generated, is it labelled?
pitfalls: '#ad' hidden among 20 hashtags at the end: ASCI says not at the end, not buried in hashtags. Put 'Ad' or 'Paid partnership' in the first line.
'#sp' or '#spon' as the only label: the FTC calls these vague and ASCI does not list them. Use 'Ad', 'Sponsored' or 'Paid partnership'.
Brand website copy in the creator's mouth ('This revolutionary formula delivers holistic nourishment'): followers smell it and engagement drops. Rewrite in the creator's own words and rhythm.
'Been using it for months' when the product arrived last week: a false endorsement. Say what is true: 'Two weeks in, here's what I noticed.'
A fitness creator saying a supplement 'cures' anything, or a finance creator promising returns: needs qualifications under ASCI Addendum II and may break SEBI rules. Cut the claim.
Gifted product posted with no label because 'it wasn't paid': ASCI counts free products as a material connection. Label it 'Free gift' or 'Collaboration'.
cards.exemplar_brief: Instagram caption plus 5 talking points for a Bengaluru fitness creator's paid collaboration with a Mysuru millet-protein brand; audience: her followers, office-goers aged 22-35; Hinglish (Roman script) in her casual voice; 80-150 words; 'Ad' label in the first line in addition to the Paid partnership tag; one honest limitation; discount code with a 7-day deadline; claims limited to the brand's approved list (12 g protein per serving).

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. The first line is 'Ad | Paid partnership with [@brand]', with a tag note. The hook is in her voice. The real-use moment is now concrete without invention (4 baje, the samosa trolley, the pack in the drawer in place of biscuits). The only claim is the approved 12 g, and the limit comes in her voice ('Mera rule: yeh snack hai, khaane ki jagah nahi'). The code runs till Thursday 22 October 11:59 pm, 7 days from a Thursday post (22 October 2026 is a Thursday). There are 3 hashtags, the caption is 102 words, and the 5 talking points give must-says and don'ts. The taste or crunch detail is a slot, which is right: only the creator can supply it. Nits (writer): the slot is written as a full instruction inside the caption instead of a short [taste in her words] mark; the second limit sentence ('12 g ek serving ka hai, poore din ka nahi') is the label hedge again, and the brief asks for one limit. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Sponsored integration / sponsor read script
cards.summary: The 30-90 second segment inside a creator's video or podcast that introduces a sponsor in the creator's own voice, discloses it out loud, ties it to the episode's topic and gives one action. Good looks like a bridge from the content so the read does not feel like a cut to an ad, one personal use moment, approved claims only, and a clean return to the episode.
use_for: YouTube video integrations (pre-roll position or mid-video)
Video and audio podcast host-read sponsor segments
Talking points for creators who prefer to ad-lib
Livestream sponsor mentions (repeated through the stream)
avoid: A standalone caption for an Instagram collab: use genre:sponsored_creator_post
A brand-produced ad that runs as media: use genre:video_ad_script or genre:radio_spot_script
Podcast ad reads written by the brand for many shows: see genre:podcast_ad_read
The episode itself: use genre:youtube_video_script or genre:podcast_script

sources.title: YouTube Help: Paid product placements, endorsements and sponsorships (read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: select the paid promotion option for sponsorships; it 'adds a disclosure label that appears at the beginning of your video'; creators and partners remain responsible for legal requirements

sources.title: ASCI Guidelines for Influencer Advertising in Digital Media (with Addendum II, 2023)
sources.supports: video label timing: up to 15 s, at least 3 s; 15 s to 2 min, a third of the length; 2 min or longer, the whole section where the brand is discussed; live streams: announce at start and end; audio: at the start, end and around every break; finance and health influencers state qualifications

sources.title: FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
sources.supports: in video, say the disclosure in the video itself, not only in the description; repeat it periodically in live streams

sources.title: Fiverr: Podcast Writing category (read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: podcast-writing gigs list 'Ad break' as a deliverable (59 gigs)

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: script writer $30-$56 per hour; script projects include commercial and advertising scripts

buyers: Brands and agencies preparing integration talking points
cards.value_why: Fiverr podcast-writing gigs list 'Ad break' writing as a deliverable (59 gigs, 2026-10-04); Upwork's script type covers commercial scripts at $30-$56/hr. Video podcasts and creator-led ads are growing in 2026, so integrations are a standing need for creators who sell sponsorships.
cards.goal: The viewer or listener stays through the segment instead of skipping, understands why the creator uses the product, and uses the code or link.

structure.does: Links from the episode's topic and says plainly that this part is sponsored ('Is video ko sponsor kiya hai ...').
Names the viewer's problem that connects the topic to the product.
What it is in one line, then how the creator uses it, with one on-screen demo moment.
The single benefit most relevant to this audience (approved claim), the offer, code and deadline.
Where to go (link in description or pinned comment) and the code said twice.
A line that hands back to the episode so viewers do not drop.
On-screen label for the whole segment (ASCI: the brand section in videos of 2 minutes or more), paid promotion box ticked, description text with link and disclosure.

length.note: Set by the sponsor contract. Time it by reading aloud at the creator's pace; Hinglish and Hindi delivery speed varies by creator.

checklist: Is the sponsorship said out loud in the first line of the segment?
Do the production notes include an on-screen label and the paid promotion setting?
Does the segment connect to the episode's topic?
Is there one personal use moment the creator can honestly say?
Is there one benefit, not a feature list?
Are all claims from the brand's approved list, with no guaranteed returns or cures?
Is the code or link said at least twice?
Read aloud, does it fit the contracted duration?
Is there a line that returns to the episode?
pitfalls: 'But first, a word from our sponsor' followed by brand copy read flat: the skip button wins. Bridge from the topic and keep the creator's normal voice.
Disclosure only in the description: the FTC wants it said in the video, and ASCI wants the label on screen for the brand section. Say it and show it.
Reading six features from the brand deck: viewers retain one. Pick the benefit that matters to this audience.
Finance or health claims ('guaranteed 12% returns', 'boosts immunity') from a creator without the qualification: breaks ASCI Addendum II and may break SEBI rules. Use approved, factual claims only.
A 2-minute read in a 10-minute video: the audience leaves. Hold to the contracted length.
Mid-roll placed before the video has delivered anything: viewers leave before the read. Place it after the first payoff.
cards.exemplar_brief: 60-second sponsor read inside a Hindi personal-finance YouTube video on emergency-fund basics, for a UPI-based recurring-deposit app; creator voice: calm, explains like a friend; Hinglish VO in Roman script; spoken disclosure in the first line plus an on-screen label for the whole segment; one demo moment (setting up a Rs 500 weekly auto-save); approved claims only, no return guarantees; promo code and description link said twice; ends with a line returning to the video topic.

verified.note: Bridge from the topic then spoken 'ye ad hai' in the opening line, on-screen label throughout, problem framed in the creator's calm voice ('dikkat plan ki nahi, yaad rakhne ki hai'), Rs 500 weekly UPI demo, one benefit, code said 3x and link 2x, clean return line ('kitna amount rakhna chahiye?'), no rate or return claim. Personal-use placeholder is correct since none was supplied.

cards.name: Stage play / nukkad natak script
cards.summary: A script for live performance, from proscenium plays to India's street theatre (nukkad natak), where a small cast with no set draws a crowd, shows a social problem through quick scenes, talks to the audience directly and ends on a slogan or pledge. Good looks like short loud-friendly lines, a chorus and songs that hold an open-air crowd, a story instead of a lecture, and one clear action at the end.
use_for: NGO and CSR awareness campaigns (cyber fraud, health, voting, sanitation, gender)
College dramatics society and inter-college competition plays
Government and civic awareness drives in markets, bastis and campuses
One-act plays for schools, festivals and corporate events
Full-length plays for theatre groups
avoid: Filmed short stories: use genre:short_film_script
A single performer's comedy: use genre:standup_comedy_set
Short filmed comic scenes: use genre:sketch_comedy
Radio or broadcast awareness messages: use genre:public_service_announcement

sources.title: Screenwriters Association (India): Script registration guidelines
sources.supports: SWA registers Story, Script and Dialogue for members (protect the play before circulating it)

sources.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (MHA text)
sources.supports: s.356 defamation (including spoken imputations), s.196 promoting enmity between groups, s.299 insulting religious beliefs

cards.value_why: Small paid market; street plays are commissioned by NGOs, colleges and awareness campaigns (harvest). Fees are modest and often bundled with performance.
cards.goal: The live audience stays to the end, reacts or joins in, and leaves able to repeat the message and do the one action.

structure.does: Drumbeat, clapping, a chant or song by the full cast to pull passers-by into a circle; names the issue in a slogan.
A narrator addresses the crowd directly, sets up the character and the problem in their own street language.
3-5 quick scenes with recognisable characters (the vegetable seller, the caller, the son); the chorus becomes crowd, wall, phone or chorus voice; freezes and tableaux mark the turns.
The consequence lands; the sutradhar stops the action and asks the audience what the character should do.
The practical action (what to say, whom to call), a slogan the crowd repeats, a closing song.
Acts and scenes with character names above dialogue and stage directions in brackets or italics; set, light and sound cues kept minimal.
structure.length: Per the running time in the brief

length.note: A nukkad natak runs short because the crowd is standing in the open; a one-act or full-length stage play runs longer. Write to the running time in the brief and time a read-through with the cast.

checklist: Does a nukkad script open with a crowd-gathering chant or song before any dialogue?
Are most lines short enough to shout clearly in the open air?
Does the sutradhar or a character address the audience directly at least twice?
Is there at least one moment where the audience is asked to respond?
Is the issue shown through a character's story rather than explained in a speech?
Are character names above dialogue and stage directions in brackets?
Can the props be carried by the cast (a dupatta, a phone, a stick)?
Does it end with one practical action and a slogan the crowd can repeat?
Does it fit the running time in the brief?
pitfalls: Long speeches by a 'wise' character: crowds drift away. Break the message into exchanges, chants and questions.
A lecture with no story: people watch a person get cheated, not a list of rules. Build the play on one character's mistake and recovery.
Quiet, subtle scenes and whispered lines: they die outdoors. Write for volume and big physical action.
Message in formal Hindi or English for a market crowd: write in the street's language and code-mixing.
Naming a real official, company or community as the villain: defamation and enmity risk under BNS. Use types, not real names.
Election-period plays on political themes performed for a party: check the Model Code of Conduct and local permissions first.
cards.exemplar_brief: 15-minute nukkad natak script in Hindi (Devanagari) for a Patna NGO's anti-cyber-fraud campaign at markets and college gates: a vegetable seller loses her savings to a fake 'KYC update' call; cast of 6 with a sutradhar and chorus; opening crowd-gathering chant, 4 short scenes, a moment where the audience is asked what she should do, and a closing pledge with the cyber-crime helpline number the NGO supplies and a repeatable slogan.

verified.note: Gathering chant, sutradhar addresses the crowd 3+ times, 4 scenes (market, fake KYC call, bank, replay done right), audience asked mid-call and at the freeze, pledge, repeatable slogan 'रुको! सोचो! फ़ोन काटो!', props the cast can carry, Bihari-flavoured 'हमरा'. Facts right: banks never ask OTP/PIN for KYC; 1930 is the national cyber-fraud helpline, kept as an NGO-supplied placeholder per the brief. About 1,100 words should play 12-15 min with crowd work; time it.

cards.name: Stand-up comedy set
cards.summary: A performer's set of bits, each built from a premise with an attitude, a setup, a punchline that lands on the last word, and tags, linked by segues and callbacks and written for this comedian's voice. Good looks like an early laugh, specific details from the performer's life, punches at power rather than communities, and a closer that ties back to earlier material.
use_for: Open-mic and club sets for new and working comics (writing and punch-up)
Material for hosts, award shows and corporate events
Roast jokes (with the subject's consent)
Brand content in a stand-up format and Reels cut from sets
avoid: Multi-character comic scenes: use genre:sketch_comedy
Written satire articles: use genre:satire_parody
Emceeing an event with running order and introductions: use genre:anchoring_script
Speeches that only need a few light lines: use genre:keynote_speech or genre:wedding_speech

sources.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (MHA text)
sources.supports: s.356 defamation, s.196 promoting enmity between groups, s.299 deliberate insult to religious beliefs: the legal risk around jokes on communities, religion and real people

buyers: Brands and creators using stand-up formats
cards.value_why: Comedians mostly write their own material; paid writing is for specials, hosts, roasts and corporate shows (harvest).
cards.goal: The audience laughs at each punch, the laughs build across the set, and the comedian can perform it as their own.

structure.does: A quick, high-certainty laugh that establishes who the comic is (often addressing how they look, sound or where they are from).
The topic plus an attitude (weird, scary, stupid, hard) and why: 'Bengaluru landlords interview tenants like they're adopting a child.'
Only the facts the audience needs, in specific details, pointing them toward a wrong assumption.
The reveal that breaks the assumption, with the funny word last; then 2-4 tags, extra punches off the same setup; an act-out where it plays.
Short links that move from one bit to the next without 'so anyway'.
The strongest bit or a callback chain to earlier bits; ends on a big laugh and the comic's name.

length.note: Open-mic slots are short, club spots longer, an hour special the top end. Time the set on stage, not on paper; marked pauses and act-outs take longer than reading.

checklist: Does the opener get to a laugh within the first few lines?
Does each bit have a premise with an attitude, not just a topic?
Does each punchline end on the funny word?
Are there tags after the main punches?
Are pauses and act-outs marked for performance?
Is the material specific to this performer's life and voice?
Is there at least one callback, ideally in the closer?
Does it fit the slot time when performed?
Does it avoid targeting a religion, caste or community, and avoid invented claims about real people?
Is every joke original (no lifted viral jokes)?
pitfalls: 'Have you noticed how traffic is bad?' with no attitude: a topic is not a premise. Add the angle: 'Bengaluru traffic is the only thing in my life that has a clear five-year plan.'
Punchline buried mid-sentence ('...which is why, funnily enough, my landlord, by the way, ...'): rewrite so the reveal word is last.
Explaining the joke after it: kills the laugh. Trust the audience and tag instead.
Lifting a viral joke or another comic's premise: comedians and audiences spot it, and the writer's credibility ends there. Write from the performer's own life.
Jokes about a religion, caste or community: legal risk under BNS ss.196 and 299, and Indian comedians have faced FIRs over material. Punch at systems, power and yourself.
Roasting a real person's private life with invented claims: defamation risk. Keep to public acts and get consent for roasts.
cards.exemplar_brief: 5-minute Hinglish stand-up set (open-mic length) for a 27-year-old Indore-born software tester now living in Bengaluru, on moving to Bengaluru and dealing with landlords; two bits, each with a premise, setup, punchline and at least 2 tags; one act-out; a callback in the closer; [PAUSE] and [ACT-OUT] cues marked; no jokes on religion, caste or community.

verified.note: Opener reaches the tester/bug persona fast; two bits with attitude premises, setups, punches and 3 tags each, [PAUSE]/[ACT-OUT] marked, the landlord-interview act-out works ('Ye to mere HR ne bhi nahi poochha!'), closer is a bug-report callback ending on 'Cannot reproduce.' Weaker: Bengaluru deposit material is well-trodden, tag 2 (FD nominee) is muddled, the bit-2 punch ends on 'padegi' rather than 'change request'.
